newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Empowerment deal to transform S.African mining industry.
newsitem.headline: Empowerment deal to transform S.African mining industry.

text.p: South Africa's mining industry, run by whites for more than a century, is being transformed, analysts said on Wednesday after a black consortium took control of major gold mining company JCI Ltd.
The country's largest corporation, Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd, on Tuesday sold its 34.9 percent controlling stake of JCI to African Mining Consortium in a $630 million deal.
Analysts said the deal to give black business control of South Africa's sixth-largest mining company could change the mining industry
"The good thing is that you have got a board of directors who come from all angles and not just the traditional white upper class," said a Johannesburg gold mining analyst who asked not to be named.
"You want to hear all the arguments and all the possibilities, (this is) what the new JCI board is going to bring in."
South Africa's mining industry -- cornerstone of the economy -- has been dominated by whites since gold was discovered more than a century ago.

With President Nelson Mandela's government in power, black South Africans are gaining a foothold in the country's economy with many large companies like Anglo American supporting black economic empowerment.

The JCI deal is the second big disposal by Anglo American to black interests. It recently sold its 35 percent stake in Johnnies Industrial Corp Ltd (Johnnic) -- an industrial holding concern -- to the National Empowerment Consortium.

"It is a path on the way to progress," Nick Goodwin, another mining analyst, said. He said the JCI deal would not empower ordinary black South Africans immediately but could help create a black economic elite.
"You have to establish an elitist black group and then will come a middle-class black group and then you will drag all these other people up with you," Goodwin said.
He said with control of JCI passing to the consortium, the company could start working on expansion and new development.
"The company (JCI) is independent now. It is not Anglo's small brother anymore," Goodwin said.

Goodwin said with South African mining companies spreading their wings across Africa following the demise of apartheid, a black chairman and board of directors could help JCI -- which already has some 37 projects underway in Africa.
"I think having a black chairman plus a black board -- black unions are involved in this now -- could open quite a lot of doors (in Africa)," Goodwin said.

The consortium, led by financial services group Capital Alliance Holdings Ltd, included Co-ordinated Network Investments, African Renaissance, the Women's Development Bank Investments and Thebe Investment Corporation.

The investment arm of the powerful National Union of Mineworkers -- the Mineworkers' Investment Company -- and the South African Clothing and Textile Workers' Union Investment Group will have a stake through the company Saflife, which holds a 50.3 percent stake in Capital Alliance.
